========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, I suppose I'm here because... honestly, my wife really pushed for it, and my director at work kind of heavily suggested it, in a way. The thing is, I just can’t seem to stop launching projects. And I know, I'm an IT manager, so planning and executing is literally my job, I've got my degree in it, it's what I do. But lately this is... it's different. It's like a switch gets flipped and I just start initiating everything all at once. 

I’m drafting these massive, sweeping work plans for the department that go way beyond my actual scope, and at the exact same time, I’m drawing up these intense, minute-by-minute study schedules for myself to knock out multiple advanced certifications in a fraction of the time it normally takes. But it doesn't stop at the office, you know? I get home and I immediately start tearing into the drywall for these huge home network upgrades—running new cable, configuring new hardware, setting up a whole new server rack. And while I'm doing all of that, I'm constantly firing off messages to old contacts, vendors, people I haven't talked to since college, just trying to get all these different initiatives off the ground. 

It just gets so incredibly intense. It's like this motor running inside me that I can't shut off, and I just completely blow past normal limits. I don't even realize how far over the line I am until my wife has to literally step in and take the crimping tool out of my hands, or my director actually has to pull me into a closed-door meeting to intervene and tell me I need to hit the brakes. So... yeah, that's why I'm sitting here. They think I need to get it checked out.

Well, normal is... I mean, what is normal, really? But if you mean, do I go back to feeling like my regular self, not supercharged and not dragging through the mud... yes, I do have those periods. There are definitely times, sometimes stretching out for a few weeks at a time, where my energy is just... stable. Calm. Flat, even, but in a good way. I'm not staying up all night re-wiring the house, and I'm not stuck in bed unable to face the day. I'm just going to work, doing my job, coming home. 

But... and this is the part that really messes with my head, doctor... even during those quiet weeks, when my mood is totally fine, the other stuff doesn't always go away. Like, I'll be sitting at my desk, feeling completely even-keeled, but I'll look at the Microsoft Teams statuses of my staff, and I'll still see the patterns. I'll still know, deep down, that when Dave goes from 'Available' to 'Away' at exactly 10:14 AM, and then Sarah sets hers to 'Do Not Disturb' two minutes later... it's a coded warning. It's a signal they're sending about me, about my job security or some audit they're planning behind my back. I know it sounds crazy when I say it out loud, but in the moment, even when I'm not manic, it feels like an absolute fact. 

And the voices, too. Not full conversations, usually, but just... brief comments. I'll be in the server room, completely alone, just doing routine maintenance, feeling totally fine, and I'll hear someone say my name, or mutter something like, "He missed a spot," or "Watch him." Just quick, little jabs. And I'll spin around, and there's absolutely no one there. The security badge reader hasn't beeped, the door is locked... it's just me and the hum of the cooling units. So, yeah, my mood might be perfectly normal, but my brain is still... processing things that aren't there. It's like the operating system is running fine, but there's this background process I can't kill that keeps throwing up these bizarre error messages. It's exhausting, honestly, because I can never fully let my guard down, even when I'm supposed to be at baseline.

And other times, I'll have one of those intense, high-voltage weeks where I'm redesigning the entire office network architecture, and when it finally wraps up, I don't crash at all. I just kind of... level out. Go back to baseline. \n\nSo, no, there isn't really a strict pattern to it, which honestly makes it so much harder to deal with. If I knew that every time I went overboard with a project I was going to pay for it with a month of depression, maybe I could try to manage it better, or at least brace myself for the impact, you know? But because it's so random... it's like living with a faulty motherboard. You never know when it's going to short out, or why. I've spent hours trying to chart it out—literally, I built a spreadsheet trying to correlate my project initiation dates with my low moods, tracking sleep hours, caffeine intake, even the weather, trying to find some kind of algorithm to explain it. But the data just doesn't line up. It's totally erratic.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're back to normal between these intense, energetic periods?\n\nPatient: Well, normal is... I mean, what is normal, really? But if you mean, do I go back to feeling like my regular self, not supercharged and not dragging through the mud... yes, I do have those periods. There are definitely times, sometimes stretching out for a few weeks at a time, where my energy is just... stable. Calm. Flat, even, but in a good way. I'm not staying up all night re-wiring the house, and I'm not stuck in bed unable to face the day. I'm just going to work, doing my job, coming home. \n\nBut... and this is the part that really messes with my head, doctor... even during those quiet weeks, when my mood is totally fine, the other stuff doesn't always go away. Like, I'll be sitting at my desk, feeling completely even-keeled, but I'll look at the Microsoft Teams statuses of my staff, and I'll still see the patterns. I'll still know, deep down, that when Dave goes from 'Available' to 'Away' at exactly 10:14 AM, and then Sarah sets hers to 'Do Not Disturb' two minutes later... it's a coded warning. It's a signal they're sending about me, about my job security or some audit they're planning behind my back. I know it sounds crazy when I say it out loud, but in the moment, even when I'm not manic, it feels like an absolute fact. \n\nAnd the voices, too. Not full conversations, usually, but just... brief comments. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, "not true" is... I mean, it’s a tricky concept, isn't it? Because in the moment, it feels like the absolute, undeniable truth. But... yes. Yes, I suppose so. Because my logical brain—the IT manager brain, the guy who deals in binary and server logs and hard data—knows that there’s evidence against what I'm thinking. My wife will point it out, or I'll even point it out to myself, but it just doesn't matter. The belief just completely overrides the facts. 

Like I was saying a minute ago about those quiet weeks, where my mood is totally fine and I’m not in a big swing either way... the paranoia, or whatever you want to call it, it just doesn't shut off. It’s the Teams statuses, sure, but it goes so much deeper than that. It’s calendar invites, too. I’ll get a totally standard Outlook invite from my director for a "Q3 Alignment Sync" or a "Quick Touchbase," and my stomach just drops. I can look at my recent performance reviews—they’re stellar, I literally got a bonus last quarter, there is physical, financial evidence that I am doing a good job—but I will look at that calendar invite and become absolutely convinced that it's a coded warning. 

And it’s not just digital, it’s in the office, too. I’ll walk past the breakroom to get coffee, and I’ll hear two of the junior devs talking in low voices, and maybe one of them says something completely innocuous like, "We need to pivot on this strategy." But my brain just locks onto it. Pivot. They’re pivoting away from me. I'll get back to my desk and I am just consumed by this absolute certainty that these hallway comments, the calendar invites, the status changes... they are all connected. I get convinced that they are actively building a case to push me out of the company. 

I’ll sit there for hours, completely ignoring my actual work, just combing through my sent folder, trying to find the exact email they’re going to use as ammunition to terminate me. I’ll map out who was in the breakroom, what time the invite was sent, trying to reverse-engineer their plot. And the crazy thing is, part of me knows I'm doing it. Part of me is screaming, "Look at your bonus check! Look at your track record! No one is firing you!" But that logical voice is just a whisper compared to this overwhelming, crushing belief that the axe is about to fall. It just... it takes over everything, even when I have all the proof in the world that I'm safe.

See things? No, no, I don't think I've ever really seen anything that wasn't there. My vision is fine, I'm not seeing people standing in the corner of the room or shadows moving or anything cinematic like that. It's not a visual thing for me. Well, time is... time gets a little distorted with this stuff, to be perfectly honest. But because I'm an IT guy, I like data, right? I like to have metrics and hard facts to look at. If I'm in the zone, pulling Cat6 cable through the living room wall at 2 AM, and my wife comes out and asks me to keep the noise down, or if a vendor takes more than an hour to reply to an email about a bulk hardware order... I just snap. It’s like this blinding flash of frustration. I get so intensely irritated, because to me, it feels like they’re intentionally throwing up roadblocks. Like everyone around me is moving in slow motion and they’re actively trying to drag me down to their speed. I know logically my wife just wants to sleep, but in the moment, it feels like she’s sabotaging my progress. So it's not just pure happiness... it’s this high-voltage energy that turns into pure rage the second someone gets in my way.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself feeling really down or depressed?\n\nPatient: Yeah... yeah, I do. And it's... it's such a jarring contrast, you know? Because when I'm up, I'm so up, but then... there are these stretches. It's like the power just cuts out. The servers crash, the network goes dark, and I'm just left sitting in the quiet. \n\nWhen it hits, I wake up and I just feel... heavy. Flat. Like all that electricity is just gone, drained out of me completely. I lie there in bed and I just feel like this absolute, failed version of myself. I look at the holes in the drywall, the half-finished server rack, the fifty emails I started drafting to vendors, and instead of feeling that drive to finish it all, I just feel this crushing weight of... I don't know, inadequacy? Like, who do I think I am, trying to do all of this? I'm just a fraud. I'm a failure. \n\nAnd getting out of bed during those times... it feels like I'm moving through wet concrete. The simplest things become monumental tasks. Even just... my wife, she'll ask me something totally normal, like what I want for dinner or if I paid the water bill, and it just feels like too much. It's overwhelming. I can't even process the question, let alone formulate an answer. I just want to pull the covers over my head and disappear. It's not just a bad day, it's this deep, sinking feeling that everything I do is pointless, and that I'm completely useless. And it can last for weeks, just this slow, agonizing slog through the days where I can barely function, let alone manage a whole IT department. It's... it's really hard to explain just how empty it feels compared to the high.\n\nDoctor: Do your low or depressed periods usually happen after one of these intense, energetic periods?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, you'd think so, right? Like, what goes up must come down, that kind of logic. You'd think the crash would always just naturally follow the... the surge, the manic energy, or whatever you want to call it. And sometimes it does, sure. Sometimes I burn the candle at both ends, running cables and drafting proposals until I literally just collapse into this heavy, dark place. But... no, it's not actually that predictable. It's not a neat little sequence of events. \n\nSometimes the darkness just creeps in out of nowhere, completely unprovoked. I could be having a totally normal week—no massive projects, no staying up till 3 AM configuring routers, just doing my regular 9-to-5, coming home, eating dinner with my wife... and then, boom. I wake up one morning and it's like someone pulled the plug on the server. Just dead. And other times, I'll have one of those intense, high-voltage weeks where I'm redesigning the entire office network architecture, and when it finally wraps up, I don't crash at all. I just kind of... level out. Go back to baseline. \n\nSo, no, there isn't really a strict pattern to it, which honestly makes it so much harder to deal with. If I knew that every time I went overboard with a project I was going to pay for it with a month of depression, maybe I could try to manage it better, or at least brace myself for the impact, you know? But because it's so random... it's like living with a faulty motherboard. You never know when it's going to short out, or why. I've spent hours trying to chart it out—literally, I built a spreadsheet trying to correlate my project initiation dates with my low moods, tracking sleep hours, caffeine intake, even the weather, trying to find some kind of algorithm to explain it. But the data just doesn't line up. It's totally erratic.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're back to normal between these intense, energetic periods?\n\nPatient: Well, normal is... I mean, what is normal, really? But if you mean, do I go back to feeling like my regular self, not supercharged and not dragging through the mud... yes, I do have those periods. There are definitely times, sometimes stretching out for a few weeks at a time, where my energy is just... stable. Calm. Flat, even, but in a good way. I'm not staying up all night re-wiring the house, and I'm not stuck in bed unable to face the day. I'm just going to work, doing my job, coming home. \n\nBut... and this is the part that really messes with my head, doctor... even during those quiet weeks, when my mood is totally fine, the other stuff doesn't always go away. Like, I'll be sitting at my desk, feeling completely even-keeled, but I'll look at the Microsoft Teams statuses of my staff, and I'll still see the patterns. I'll still know, deep down, that when Dave goes from 'Available' to 'Away' at exactly 10:14 AM, and then Sarah sets hers to 'Do Not Disturb' two minutes later... it's a coded warning. It's a signal they're sending about me, about my job security or some audit they're planning behind my back. I know it sounds crazy when I say it out loud, but in the moment, even when I'm not manic, it feels like an absolute fact. \n\nAnd the voices, too. Not full conversations, usually, but just... brief comments. I'll be in the server room, completely alone, just doing routine maintenance, feeling totally fine, and I'll hear someone say my name, or mutter something like, \"He missed a spot,\" or \"Watch him.\" Just quick, little jabs. And I'll spin around, and there's absolutely no one there. The security badge reader hasn't beeped, the door is locked... it's just me and the hum of the cooling units. So, yeah, my mood might be perfectly normal, but my brain is still... processing things that aren't there. It's like the operating system is running fine, but there's this background process I can't kill that keeps throwing up these bizarre error messages. It's exhausting, honestly, because I can never fully let my guard down, even when I'm supposed to be at baseline.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever believe things that aren't true, even when there's evidence to the contrary?\n\nPatient: Well, \"not true\" is... I mean, it’s a tricky concept, isn't it? Because in the moment, it feels like the absolute, undeniable truth. But... yes. Yes, I suppose so. Because my logical brain—the IT manager brain, the guy who deals in binary and server logs and hard data—knows that there’s evidence against what I'm thinking. My wife will point it out, or I'll even point it out to myself, but it just doesn't matter. The belief just completely overrides the facts. \n\nLike I was saying a minute ago about those quiet weeks, where my mood is totally fine and I’m not in a big swing either way... the paranoia, or whatever you want to call it, it just doesn't shut off. I can look at my recent performance reviews—they’re stellar, I literally got a bonus last quarter, there is physical, financial evidence that I am doing a good job—but I will look at that calendar invite and become absolutely convinced that it's a coded warning. \n\nAnd it’s not just digital, it’s in the office, too. I’ll walk past the breakroom to get coffee, and I’ll hear two of the junior devs talking in low voices, and maybe one of them says something completely innocuous like, \"We need to pivot on this strategy.\" But my brain just locks onto it. Pivot. They’re pivoting away from me. I'll get back to my desk and I am just consumed by this absolute certainty that these hallway comments, the calendar invites, the status changes... they are all connected. I get convinced that they are actively building a case to push me out of the company. \n\nI’ll sit there for hours, completely ignoring my actual work, just combing through my sent folder, trying to find the exact email they’re going to use as ammunition to terminate me. I’ll map out who was in the breakroom, what time the invite was sent, trying to reverse-engineer their plot. And the crazy thing is, part of me knows I'm doing it. Part of me is screaming, \"Look at your bonus check! Look at your track record! No one is firing you!\" But that logical voice is just a whisper compared to this overwhelming, crushing belief that the axe is about to fall. It just... it takes over everything, even when I have all the proof in the world that I'm safe.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever see things that aren't there?\n\nPatient: See things? No, no, I don't think I've ever really seen anything that wasn't there. My vision is fine, I'm not seeing people standing in the corner of the room or shadows moving or anything cinematic like that. It's not a visual thing for me. But... well, like I was saying a few minutes ago about the server room, it's the sounds. It's hearing things. That's the part that really gets me, and it's just so incredibly distracting.\n\nIt’s almost always embedded in the background noise. Like, you know how a server room sounds, right? Or maybe you don't, but it's this constant, heavy hum. We've got these massive HVAC units keeping the server racks cool, plus all the high-RPM fans on the hardware spinning at once. It's just a solid wall of white noise. Just my name, spoken right behind my ear. Or it'll be these short, clipped little comments. Someone muttering, \"check the logs,\" or... or \"they know.\" \n\n\"They know.\" That one really, really gets under my skin, especially with everything else I was telling you about the Teams statuses and the calendar invites. My wife is asleep, the doors are deadbolted. But I'll hear \"they know\" coming from just over my left shoulder. \n\nAnd I'll completely freeze. Legal trouble? No, no, thankfully I've managed to avoid anything with the police or the courts. But... the job and the relationships? Yeah. Yeah, it’s definitely taken a toll. 

I mean, I haven't been outright fired, but I was actually put on mandatory administrative leave recently. It was right after this massive database migration we were doing. I was up for days, completely bypassing our standard QA protocols because I was just so utterly convinced I had optimized the deployment pipeline perfectly and that everyone else would just slow me down. But I was moving too fast. I missed a critical dependency, and the whole migration completely failed. It took down our primary client portal for hours. My director had to put me on leave to "recenter," which... well, it was humiliating. Especially with how paranoid I get about my job security anyway.

If I’m in one of those intense periods, I’ll commit to a dozen extra volunteer shifts and then completely blow them off because I got obsessed with a new coding project, or I’ll show up to climbing and just be totally reckless and talk everyone's ear off until they're uncomfortable. And then, of course, the crash comes, and I can't even get out of bed. I just can't follow through on anything consistently, so I just... I had to drop it all.
